Wireless World, 1979–80 · running in MAME

PSI COMP80 Screens

The PSI COMP80 was a Z80 computer designed by J. H. Adams and published as a build-it-yourself series, “A scientific computer”, in Wireless World. The six parts ran monthly from April to September 1979. Two follow-up articles on the monitors appeared in January and February 1980, and a two-part floppy disc extension in October and December 1980.

This MAME driver runs the computer’s 3 KB monitor ROM, typed back in from the magazine’s hex listing. Every picture below is a screenshot from the emulator, and every program loads from a cassette tape image or the floppy disc.

  • Z80 at 2 MHz
  • 64 × 32 characters, 6 × 10 dots each
  • 5 KB RAM from 0C00
  • Tape 300 baud, 1200 / 2400 Hz

The kit

Powertran sold the computer as a kit. The leaflet calls it the “PSI COMP 80, Z80 based computer” and shows the finished machine: a keyboard with a separate hex keypad, READY and DATA IN lamps, and a television as the display.

The kit in these photos, still in its box with the leaflet, drawings, corrections sheet, case and bagged parts, was offered for sale on eBay. The main board has been assembled.

Starting a program

c80.sh starts the emulator straight into a program: it puts the program in memory and types the command for you. The command under each screen starts it. Add MAME options after the name, for example -nowindow for full screen.

~/localdev/psicomp80/c80.sh life      # or boat, schmitt, alph, list, disk, forth, forthlife, mandel, ready

To load from the cassette image the way the real machine would, use the tape commands further down.

The monitor

Commands are a word, a space and hex addresses. A command runs as soon as its last digit is typed, with no Return.

Game of Life

Conway’s Life on a 128 × 64 board that wraps at the edges. Each character cell shows four cells using the quadrant block graphics. Written in Z80 assembly; about 0.65 s per generation in the emulator.

  • R new random board
  • P pause / resume
  • S stop, back to the monitor
Or load it from tape
cd ~/localdev/mame && ./mamed psicomp80 -cass ~/localdev/psicomp80/life/life.wav -autoboot_script ~/localdev/psicomp80/autorun.lua

Fig. 22 pictures

Recreations of the two pictorial displays photographed for Wireless World, August 1979, drawn with the COMP80 graphics characters. A third picture, the screen on the cover of the kit leaflet, is at the top of the page.

Or load it from tape
cd ~/localdev/mame && ./mamed psicomp80 -cass ~/localdev/psicomp80/pictures/boat.wav -autoboot_script ~/localdev/psicomp80/autorun.lua
cd ~/localdev/mame && ./mamed psicomp80 -cass ~/localdev/psicomp80/pictures/schmitt.wav -autoboot_script ~/localdev/psicomp80/autorun.lua

Floppy disc

The disc extension from Wireless World, October and December 1980: an FD1771 controller and an 8in drive holding about 250 KB in the IBM 3740 format. The disc software from the December article is typed in at 1D00. The program disc holds everything above. FORMAT needs the 32 KB memory expansion, so it runs on the second machine, started with c80.sh 32k disk.

Or load it from tape
cd ~/localdev/mame && C80_ADDR=1D00 ./mamed psicomp80 -cass ~/localdev/psicomp80/disk/fdos.wav -flop ~/localdev/psicomp80/disk/programs.img -autoboot_script ~/localdev/psicomp80/autorun.lua

FORTH

A second ROM puts a small FORTH in the 2 KB that held BURP; the monitor is unchanged. It has about 60 words: stack and arithmetic words, : and ;, variables and constants, IF, BEGIN and DO loops, and AT, EMIT and KEY for the screen and keyboard. Numbers are 16-bit integers. The emulator offers the ROM as a BIOS option, -bios forth; press RS at READY to enter FORTH, as you would for BURP.

  • ^ rub out (Backspace in MAME)
  • Return run the line
  • any key: stop a running word, back to READY
  • ^ at READY: back to FORTH, words kept

Game of Life in FORTH

The same game written in FORTH: 64 × 31 cells, one per character, with wrapping edges. It reads the board straight from screen memory and adds up columns of three cells first, so each cell then takes three additions. A generation takes about 3 s in the emulator; the assembly version does four times as many cells in 0.65 s. c80.sh types the program in, a line at a time, and runs it.

The program, forth/examples/life.fs
( GAME OF LIFE IN COMP80 FORTH )
( 64 X 31 CELLS ON SCREEN LINES 1-31, EDGES WRAP )
( N LIFE  RUNS N GENERATIONS FROM A RANDOM BOARD )
HEX 8040 CONSTANT SCR DECIMAL
31 CONSTANT ROWS
79 CONSTANT ALIVE  ( GRAPHIC 15: A SOLID BLOCK )
VARIABLE SEED  1979 SEED !
: RND ( -- N ) SEED @ 31421 * 6927 + DUP SEED ! ;
VARIABLE NEW  ROWS 64 * 2 - ALLOT  ( NEXT GENERATION )
VARIABLE SUMS  64 ALLOT  ( COLUMN SUMS, WRAPPED ONE EACH END )
VARIABLE UP  VARIABLE MID  VARIABLE DN
: ROW ( Y -- ADDR ) 64 * SCR + ;
: ROWS! ( Y -- ) DUP ROW MID !
  DUP DUP 0= IF ROWS + THEN 1- ROW UP !
  1+ DUP ROWS = IF DROP 0 THEN ROW DN ! ;
( A CELL IS 79 OR 32, SO A SUM OF 9 IS 288 + 47 * LIVE CELLS )
: COLSUMS ( -- ) 64 0 DO UP @ I + C@  MID @ I + C@ +
  DN @ I + C@ +  SUMS 1+ I + C! LOOP
  SUMS 64 + C@ SUMS C!  SUMS 1+ C@ SUMS 65 + C! ;
( 3 LIVE IN THE 3X3 SQUARE MEANS ALIVE, 4 MEANS NO CHANGE )
: CELL ( X -- C ) DUP SUMS + DUP C@  OVER 1+ C@ +  SWAP 2 + C@ +
  DUP 429 = IF DROP DROP ALIVE EXIT THEN
  476 = IF MID @ + C@ ELSE DROP 32 THEN ;
: GEN ( -- ) NEW  ROWS 0 DO I ROWS! COLSUMS
  64 0 DO I CELL OVER C! 1+ LOOP LOOP DROP
  ROWS 64 * 0 DO NEW I + @  SCR I + ! 2 +LOOP ;
: RANDOM ( -- ) ROWS 64 * 0 DO
  RND 0< IF ALIVE ELSE 32 THEN  SCR I + C! LOOP ;
: LIFE ( N -- ) PAGE RANDOM
  0 DO 50 0 AT ." GEN " I 1+ . GEN LOOP ;

Mandelbrot set in FORTH

One point per character, shaded by how many steps it takes to escape, with the set itself in solid blocks. With only 16-bit integers it works in fixed point with 90 as 1.0, the largest scale at which 2.0 squared still fits. The 1,984 points take about 95 s in the emulator.

The program, forth/examples/mandel.fs
( MANDELBROT SET IN COMP80 FORTH )
( ONE POINT PER CHARACTER, SHADED BY HOW SOON IT ESCAPES )
( FIXED POINT: 90 IS 1.0, SO 2.0 SQUARED STILL FITS 16 BITS )
90 CONSTANT S
24 CONSTANT MAXIT
HEX 8040 CONSTANT SCR DECIMAL
VARIABLE X  VARIABLE Y  VARIABLE CX  VARIABLE CY
: SQ ( A -- A*A ) DUP * S / ;
: SMALL ( A -- F ) DUP 0< IF NEGATE THEN 182 < ;
( ONE STEP OF Z = Z*Z + C; FALSE ONCE Z HAS ESCAPED )
: STEP ( -- F ) X @ SMALL  Y @ SMALL  AND 0= IF 0 EXIT THEN
  X @ SQ  Y @ SQ  OVER OVER + 360 > IF DROP DROP 0 EXIT THEN
  - CX @ +  X @ Y @ * S / DUP + CY @ + Y !  X ! -1 ;
: ITER ( -- N ) 0 X ! 0 Y ! 0
  BEGIN DUP MAXIT < WHILE STEP WHILE 1+ REPEAT THEN ;
( SHADES FOR 1 TO 9 STEPS; 79 IS A SOLID BLOCK, FOR THE SET )
VARIABLE PAL  32 PAL !  46 , 58 , 45 , 61 , 43 , 42 , 35 , 37 ,
: SHADE ( N -- C ) DUP MAXIT = IF DROP 79 EXIT THEN
  1- DUP 8 > IF DROP 8 THEN  DUP + PAL + @ ;
( COLUMN 0-63 TO X -2.0 TO 0.6, ROW 0-30 TO Y -1.05 TO 1.05 )
: POINT ( COL ROW -- C ) 189 * 30 / 94 - CY !
  234 * 63 / 180 - CX !  ITER SHADE ;
: MANDEL ( -- ) PAGE  31 0 DO 64 0 DO
  I J POINT  J 64 * I + SCR + C! LOOP LOOP  56 0 AT ." DONE" ;

LISP

A third ROM does the same with LISP: a LISP 1.5 style interpreter with garbage collection, recursion, LAMBDA and dynamic scope in the 2 KB that held BURP. It runs the classic LISP programs: symbolic differentiation, the Towers of Hanoi and the eight queens. The emulator offers it as -bios lisp; press RS at READY to enter it. COMP80 LISP has the language, the programs and how it works.

Screens are 384 × 320 dots, shown stretched to 4:3 the way a 1979 television would show them. Tape images live in the psicomp80 repository next to their source.
